The form collects personal information.

entries.counted with: a piece of information, a bit of information, an item of information
entries.contrast: ✗ informations and ✗ an information are among the most frequent errors made by speakers of Russian, French, German, and Spanish, in all of which the word is countable. English has no plural for it at all.

I need some advice about the contract.

The best advice I ever got came from my first boss.

senses.head: Recommendations about what to do
examples: Let me give you one piece of advice.
Her advice was to wait a week.
He never takes advice from anyone.
I need some advice about the contract.

entries.counted with: a piece of advice, a word of advice, some advice
entries.contrast: ✗ advices and ✗ an advice are wrong. Note also the noun/verb pair: the noun advice /ədˈvaɪs/ ends in /s/, the verb advise /ədˈvaɪz/ in /z/. Different spelling, different sound, constantly confused.

entries.meaning: The movable objects that make a room usable — chairs, tables, beds.

entries.counted with: a piece of furniture, an item of furniture
entries.contrast: ✗ furnitures and ✗ a furniture are wrong. This is the classic example of an uncountable noun naming things you can obviously count individually — English packages them as a mass anyway. To name one, use the specific word: a chair, a table, a desk.

entries.counted with: a piece of luggage, a bag, a suitcase

entries.contrast: ✗ luggages and ✗ a luggage are wrong. For a single item say a bag or a suitcase. Baggage has the same grammar and an extra figurative sense — emotional baggage.

entries.counted with: a piece of equipment, an item of equipment

entries.agreement: singular verb — the homework is due Friday
entries.counted with: a piece of homework, an assignment
entries.contrast: ✗ homeworks and ✗ a homework are wrong. For one task say an assignment. Note that work itself is uncountable in the same way, but works exists with different meanings — see work.

senses.head: Systematic investigation
examples: Her research focuses on sleep and memory.
More research is needed.
The research was funded by the university.
He published two pieces of research that year.

senses.head: Looking into something informally

A little research would have saved them a lot of money.

entries.countability: uncountable — no plural in standard use
entries.agreement: singular verb — the research is ongoing
entries.counted with: a piece of research, a study
entries.variants: researches exists in older and some technical writing but sounds dated
entries.contrast: ✗ researches is best avoided; say studies for countable units. American English stresses the noun on the first syllable and the verb on the second: REE-surch the noun, rih-SURCH the verb — though both stresses are heard for both.

Police collected three items of evidence from the scene.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the evidence is overwhelming
entries.counted with: a piece of evidence, an item of evidence
entries.contrast: ✗ evidences and ✗ an evidence are wrong in ordinary use. Note the fixed legal phrase Exhibit A for a numbered item, and that proof is likewise uncountable.

entries.meaning: Facts establishing that something is true.
examples: Do you have any proof of that?

There is no proof either way.

senses.head: Conclusive evidence
examples: Do you have any proof of that?
The receipt is proof of purchase.
There is no proof either way.

senses.head: A demonstration in mathematics or logic
examples: The proof runs to eighty pages.
Both proofs rely on the same lemma.

senses.head: A trial print of a text or photograph
examples: She marked up the proofs in red.

entries.countability: uncountable in the main sense; countable as a printed draft
entries.agreement: singular verb — the proof is conclusive
entries.counted with: a piece of proof
entries.contrast: In the sense 'evidence' the word is uncountable — ✗ two proofs that he was there. In mathematics and printing it is countable: a proof, two proofs. Related to evidence but stronger: evidence supports, proof settles.

entries.meaning: Facts, information, and skills acquired through experience or education.
examples: His knowledge of the period is remarkable.

To my knowledge, nobody has complained.
It happened without my knowledge.
Scientific knowledge advances by argument.

senses.head: What someone knows
examples: His knowledge of the period is remarkable.
She has a working knowledge of three languages.
The job requires knowledge of both systems.

senses.head: Awareness of a fact
examples: To my knowledge, nobody has complained.
It happened without my knowledge.

senses.head: Human understanding in general
examples: Scientific knowledge advances by argument.

entries.agreement: singular verb — his knowledge is impressive
entries.counted with: a body of knowledge, an area of knowledge
entries.variants: takes a only when modified — a good knowledge of Spanish
entries.contrast: ✗ knowledges is wrong. The one place a appears is before a modified knowledge of something: a working knowledge of French, a deep knowledge of the subject. That construction is standard and worth learning as a unit.

entries.meaning: A medium of exchange; wealth.

senses.head: Currency and wealth
examples: The money is already in your account.

Money doesn't grow on trees.

entries.counted with: a sum of money, an amount of money
entries.variants: monies (also moneys) exists in legal and financial writing, meaning separate sums
entries.contrast: The trap for Russian speakers is agreement: Russian деньги is plural, English money is singular. Say the money is on the table, never ✗ the money are. The technical plural monies means distinct funds, not banknotes.

entries.meaning: Money in the form of coins and notes.
examples: I don't have any cash on me.

senses.head: Physical money
examples: I don't have any cash on me.
The cash is kept in the safe overnight.
He paid cash for the whole thing.
They found a large amount of cash in the trunk.

senses.head: Available funds
examples: The company is short of cash this quarter.
Cash flow is the real problem.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the cash is in the safe
entries.counted with: an amount of cash, a sum of cash
entries.contrast: ✗ cashes is wrong as a noun. Cash means physical money specifically, as opposed to cards or credit — do you take cash?

entries.meaning: The baked food made from flour.

examples: We're out of bread.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the bread is fresh
entries.counted with: a loaf of bread, a slice of bread, a piece of bread
entries.variants: breads occurs when contrasting types — the breads of Italy
entries.contrast: ✗ a bread is wrong for one loaf — say a loaf of bread. The partitive matters: a slice for a cut piece, a loaf for the whole thing. Most foods behave this way: a slice of cheese, a bar of chocolate, a grain of rice.

entries.counted with: a grain of rice, a cup of rice, a bowl of rice
entries.contrast: ✗ rices is wrong. Grains and powders are uncountable in English: rice, flour, sugar, salt, sand, dust. Count them with a grain of or a measure.

entries.contrast: ✗ a sugar is wrong for the substance, though in a café two sugars is a normal way to ask for two spoonfuls or packets — a common informal exception.

She's the salt of the earth.

entries.counted with: a pinch of salt, a grain of salt, a teaspoon of salt
entries.variants: salts is countable in chemistry, meaning ionic compounds, and in bath salts, smelling salts
entries.contrast: ✗ a salt is wrong for the seasoning. In chemistry a salt is any compound of that class, and there the plural is normal.

examples: Progress has been slower than expected.
She's making good progress in Spanish.
Little progress was made at the meeting.
Any progress on the report?

With any luck, we'll be there by six.
Good luck on the exam.

entries.counted with: a tube of toothpaste
entries.contrast: ✗ a toothpaste is wrong — say a tube of toothpaste. All the paste and cream products behave this way: toothpaste, shampoo, lotion, sunscreen.

entries.meaning: Things or material of any kind. Informal.
examples: Put your stuff in the back.
There's too much stuff in this room.
What is all this stuff?
She took her stuff and left.
What is that black stuff on the ceiling?

senses.head: Things generally
examples: Put your stuff in the back.
There's too much stuff in this room.
What is all this stuff?
She took her stuff and left.

senses.head: A substance or material
examples: What is that black stuff on the ceiling?

entries.agreement: singular verb — this stuff is heavy
entries.counted with: a piece of stuff is unnatural — use a thing
entries.contrast: ✗ stuffs is wrong in modern use. This is the informal all-purpose uncountable, and it is extremely common in American speech: put your stuff over there.

entries.meaning: The body of words someone knows or a language has.
examples: Her English vocabulary is enormous.
Reading builds vocabulary faster than drilling.
He has the vocabulary of a native speaker.
The textbook has vocabularies at the back of each chapter.
Specialized vocabularies differ sharply between fields.

senses.head: Someone's stock of words
examples: Her English vocabulary is enormous.
Reading builds vocabulary faster than drilling.
He has the vocabulary of a native speaker.

senses.head: A word list
examples: The textbook has vocabularies at the back of each chapter.
Specialized vocabularies differ sharply between fields.

entries.countability: uncountable as a stock of words; countable as a list
entries.agreement: singular verb — her vocabulary is enormous
entries.counted with: an item of vocabulary, a word
entries.contrast: ✗ vocabularies meaning someone's stock of words is odd — say vocabulary. The countable sense means the word list of a language or a book.

entries.meaning: The rules of a language; a book describing them.
examples: English grammar is simpler than its spelling.
Her grammar is nearly perfect.
That's a fine point of grammar.
He owns three grammars of Old English.
Both grammars disagree on that point.

senses.head: The system of rules
examples: English grammar is simpler than its spelling.
Her grammar is nearly perfect.
That's a fine point of grammar.

senses.head: A descriptive book
examples: He owns three grammars of Old English.
Both grammars disagree on that point.

entries.countability: uncountable as a system; countable as a book or a description
entries.agreement: singular verb — English grammar is not that hard
entries.counted with: a point of grammar, a rule of grammar
entries.contrast: ✗ grammars meaning the rules is wrong — say grammar. The countable sense means a book describing them: a reference grammar of Russian.

entries.meaning: The way a word is said; someone's way of speaking.
examples: His pronunciation is nearly native.
Pronunciation is harder to fix than grammar.

senses.head: Someone's way of speaking

Pronunciation is harder to fix than grammar.
She works on pronunciation every day.

examples: The dictionary lists two pronunciations for it.
Both pronunciations are accepted.

entries.countability: uncountable as a skill; countable as variants of a word
entries.agreement: singular verb — his pronunciation is excellent
entries.counted with: a point of pronunciation
entries.contrast: The spelling is the trap: pronunciation has no o in the second syllable, unlike the verb pronounce. ✗ Pronounciation is a misspelling.

entries.meaning: The state of resting unconsciously.
examples: Sleep is the first thing to go.

She needs eight hours of sleep.

Lack of sleep affects everything.

senses.head: The state
examples: Sleep is the first thing to go.
I didn't get much sleep last night.
She needs eight hours of sleep.
He fell into a deep sleep.
Lack of sleep affects everything.

entries.agreement: singular verb — sleep is important
entries.counted with: a night's sleep, an hour of sleep
entries.contrast: ✗ sleeps is wrong as a noun. Say a good night's sleep or a nap. Note that a sleep is used in computing — the process went to sleep — but not of people.

entries.meaning: The state of being well.
examples: Her health has improved since the surgery.

He retired for health reasons.
Mental health is finally being taken seriously.
The plant is in poor health.

senses.head: Physical or mental condition
examples: Her health has improved since the surgery.
Health care is the biggest expense.
He retired for health reasons.
Mental health is finally being taken seriously.
The plant is in poor health.

entries.agreement: singular verb — her health is improving
entries.counted with: a state of health
entries.contrast: ✗ healths is wrong. The adjective is healthy; healthful describes something that promotes health.

entries.meaning: Deep affection.
examples: Love is more complicated than the songs suggest.
She fell in love with the city immediately.
He has enormous love for his students.
There was no love lost between them.
Sailing is one of his great loves.

senses.head: The emotion
examples: Love is more complicated than the songs suggest.
She fell in love with the city immediately.
He has enormous love for his students.
There was no love lost between them.

senses.head: A person or thing loved
examples: Sailing is one of his great loves.

entries.countability: uncountable — no plural in the main sense
entries.agreement: singular verb — love is complicated
entries.counted with: a feeling of love
entries.variants: loves is used of things one loves — sailing is one of his great loves
entries.contrast: ✗ A love meaning the emotion is wrong. The countable sense means a person or thing loved: she was his first love.

entries.meaning: The strong feeling of displeasure.
examples: His anger was obvious to everyone.

senses.head: The emotion
examples: His anger was obvious to everyone.
She spoke in anger and regretted it.
There is a lot of public anger about the decision.
He struggles to control his anger.
Anger is rarely a useful guide.

entries.agreement: singular verb — his anger was obvious
entries.counted with: a fit of anger, a surge of anger
entries.contrast: ✗ An anger and ✗ angers are wrong. All the raw emotions behave this way: anger, joy, grief, envy, jealousy, rage.

entries.meaning: The state of being happy.
examples: Happiness is more elusive than people expect.

Her happiness was obvious.
They wished the couple every happiness.
The pursuit of happiness is in the Declaration.

senses.head: The state
examples: Happiness is more elusive than people expect.
Money contributes to happiness only up to a point.
Her happiness was obvious.
They wished the couple every happiness.
The pursuit of happiness is in the Declaration.

entries.agreement: singular verb — happiness is elusive
entries.counted with: a state of happiness
entries.contrast: ✗ A happiness and ✗ happinesses are wrong. Every -ness abstract noun is uncountable: happiness, kindness, sadness, darkness, illness (though an illness is countable), weakness (also countable as a fault).

entries.meaning: The state of being free; a specific right.
examples: Freedom is not the same as the absence of rules.

Both freedoms were suspended during the emergency.

examples: Freedom is not the same as the absence of rules.
They fought for freedom for thirty years.
She values her freedom above everything.

senses.head: A specific liberty
examples: The constitution guarantees several freedoms.
Both freedoms were suspended during the emergency.

entries.countability: uncountable as the condition; countable as a specific liberty
entries.agreement: singular verb — freedom is not free
entries.counted with: a degree of freedom
entries.contrast: The condition is uncountable — they fought for freedom. Specific rights are countable — the freedoms guaranteed by the constitution.

entries.meaning: Fairness; the administration of law; also a judge.
examples: Justice was finally done after twelve years.
There is no justice in that outcome.
She has a strong sense of justice.
The nine justices heard arguments in October.
Both justices dissented.

senses.head: Fairness and the law
examples: Justice was finally done after twelve years.
There is no justice in that outcome.
She has a strong sense of justice.

senses.head: A high-court judge
examples: The nine justices heard arguments in October.
Both justices dissented.

entries.countability: uncountable as the principle; countable as a judge
entries.agreement: singular verb — justice was done
entries.counted with: a sense of justice
entries.contrast: ✗ Justices meaning fairness is wrong. The countable a justice means a judge of a high court: the nine justices of the Supreme Court.

entries.meaning: The absence of war; quiet and calm.
examples: Peace held for almost a decade.
The talks produced a fragile peace.
Both sides claimed to want peace.
She wanted nothing but peace and quiet.
He finally made peace with the decision.

senses.head: The absence of conflict
examples: Peace held for almost a decade.
The talks produced a fragile peace.
Both sides claimed to want peace.

senses.head: Quiet and calm
examples: She wanted nothing but peace and quiet.
He finally made peace with the decision.

entries.agreement: singular verb — peace is fragile
entries.counted with: a period of peace
entries.contrast: ✗ A peace is wrong except in the fixed diplomatic sense a peace treaty or a lasting peace. A homophone of piece, which is fully countable — see piece.

entries.meaning: The absence of sound; a particular pause.
examples: The silence in the room was total.
He listened in complete silence.
Her silence on the subject was telling.
There was an awkward silence.
Both silences lasted uncomfortably long.

senses.head: The absence of sound
examples: The silence in the room was total.
He listened in complete silence.
Her silence on the subject was telling.

senses.head: A particular pause
examples: There was an awkward silence.
Both silences lasted uncomfortably long.

entries.countability: uncountable as the absence of sound; countable as a particular pause
entries.agreement: singular verb — the silence was total
entries.counted with: a moment of silence
entries.contrast: The general absence of sound is uncountable. A particular pause is countable — an awkward silence, a long silence followed.

entries.meaning: The absence of light.
examples: The darkness was total once the lamp went out.

He is afraid of the darkness.
They worked on in near darkness.
Darkness comes early in December.

senses.head: The absence of light
examples: The darkness was total once the lamp went out.
She waited until darkness fell.
He is afraid of the darkness.
They worked on in near darkness.
Darkness comes early in December.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the darkness was total
entries.counted with: a degree of darkness
entries.contrast: ✗ A darkness and ✗ darknesses are wrong outside poetry. Like all -ness nouns, this is uncountable.

entries.meaning: Mental strain; also emphasis on a syllable, or physical force.

The word has two stresses.
Primary stress falls on the first syllable.

senses.head: Mental strain
examples: Stress is cumulative, not episodic.

The job comes with a lot of stress.

senses.head: Emphasis on a syllable
examples: The word has two stresses.
Primary stress falls on the first syllable.

entries.countability: uncountable as strain; countable in phonetics and engineering
entries.agreement: singular verb — stress is cumulative
entries.counted with: a source of stress, a level of stress
entries.contrast: The psychological sense is uncountable — ✗ he has many stresses is odd; say a lot of stress. Phonetics and engineering do count: primary and secondary stresses.

entries.meaning: Physical force; also demands or strain.
examples: Check the tire pressure.

Water pressure dropped overnight.
The pressure to publish is enormous.
Both pressures — money and time — hit at once.

senses.head: Physical force
examples: Check the tire pressure.
Blood pressure was normal.
Water pressure dropped overnight.

senses.head: Demands or strain
examples: The pressure to publish is enormous.
Both pressures — money and time — hit at once.

entries.countability: uncountable as force or strain; countable as specific demands
entries.agreement: singular verb — the pressure was enormous
entries.counted with: a level of pressure
entries.contrast: Physical force and general strain are uncountable. Specific demands are countable and usually plural: the pressures of the job.

entries.meaning: Regard for someone; also an aspect or particular.

senses.head: Regard for someone
examples: Respect has to be earned.

He showed no respect for the process.

examples: In many respects the plan is sound.

entries.counted with: a great deal of respect
entries.contrast: Regard for someone is uncountable — ✗ many respects does not mean much admiration. The countable respect means an aspect or particular: in many respects, the plan is sound.

entries.meaning: Confidence in someone; also a legal financial arrangement.

examples: Trust takes years to build and a moment to lose.

entries.meaning: Satisfaction in an achievement; also excessive self-regard.

The garden is a source of great pride.

senses.head: The emotion
examples: He felt no shame whatsoever.

examples: Guilt kept him awake for weeks.
